findings.title: Conflicting providers with equal order are now silently resolved instead of failing
findings.body: Before this change, finding more than one CryptoProvider was a hard error. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If two of them are on the classpath (for example FIPS and default/BC), the winner is whatever ServiceLoader returns first, because the sort is stable. Only a debug log records the ignored providers. A misconfigured deployment can therefore run non-FIPS crypto when FIPS was intended, with no visible error. Ties at the highest order should still raise an error, or these providers should get distinct orders.

findings.title: Ignored providers are still instantiated, with global Security side effects
findings.body: Sorting by `order()` requires ServiceLoader to instantiate every CryptoProvider on the classpath. The constructors have JVM-wide side effects: DefaultCryptoProvider calls `Security.addProvider(BC)`, and FIPS1402Provider inserts KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider, BCFIPS and BCJSSE at positions 1-3 and rewrites the ssl.*ManagerFactory security properties. These run even for providers that are then ignored. Previously this setup was rejected outright. Now the JVM security configuration is altered by providers that are not used. Expose order without instantiation (e.g. `ServiceLoader.stream()` with an annotation or static metadata), or keep ambiguous setups as an error.

findings.title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order()` is added as an abstract method on a public SPI interface. Any third-party or downstream CryptoProvider implementation, including the separately released keycloak-client repo this is meant to sync with, will fail to compile or throw AbstractMethodError at runtime. Making it a `default` method returning a baseline value would keep compatibility.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, and the round trip is never checked against JCA
findings.body: `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` generates a key on the default curve (P-256) for every test. ES384 and ES512 are therefore exercised with 32-byte r/s values, never with the 48- or 66-byte values those algorithms produce; the P-521 case, where values can have a leading 0x00 and exceed the length, is not covered. The test also only checks that DER->RS->DER->RS is self-consistent. It never verifies that the DER produced by `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` is accepted by `Signature.verify`, or that it equals the original JCA DER. An encoder bug that is symmetric with the decoder would pass. Initialize the generator with the matching curve and verify the re-encoded signature.

findings.title: Dead encoder calls and no input length validation in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 build ASN1Encoder instances and discard them; this is leftover dead code. The method also never checks that `signature.length == signLength`. A malformed or truncated JWS signature surfaces as an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than the declared IOException, which callers may not handle.
